title: Weekly Deep Dive: Three Near-Misses in Seven Days — Is US Air Traffic Control Breaking Down?
summary: Three serious near-miss incidents in a single week — Miami, LAX, and John Wayne Airport — have aviation watchers asking if this is a statistical blip or a system finally buckling under years of controller shortages and post-COVID strain. Ryan and Hope dig into the history of ATC staffing crises, what the FAA and NTSB can actually do about it, and why this might be the moment airport capacity plans hit a wall.

topic.topic: Multiple near-miss collisions at major US airports in two weeks signal a systemic air traffic control or pilot communication breakdown.
topic.why: Three serious near-miss incidents (Miami Lufthansa/American, LAX Air France/American, John Wayne Cessna jet blast) in 7 days across top-tier airports represent an unusual spike. This isn't isolated mechanic failures or weather—it's execution failures at the human/system interface with potential regulatory and operational consequences that will reshape procedures, training, and possibly ATC staffing for years.
key_facts: Lufthansa 747 and American 787 came within critical distance in Miami; Air France A350 and American A321 came within 400 feet at LAX in same week
Third incident: Cessna flipped by jet blast at John Wayne Airport same weekend, raising questions about ground operations and runway spacing
All three involved major carriers at congested hub airports with heavy traffic and complex airspace
Pattern suggests communication failures, procedural gaps, or controller workload issues rather than random events
No fatalities but near-miss severity forces FAA/NTSB into mandatory review of ATC procedures, pilot training, and potentially staffing levels
